summary: The original Remote Direct Data Placement RFCs did not create IANA registries for error, operation, and function codes. This RFC creates them, fills them with existing values, and gives assignment guidance for future ones.

eli5.summary: A numbered list of codes that was never kept. This starts the official list and says how new codes get added.

questions: how are rddp error codes structured
subtitle: Official code registries for Remote Direct Data Placement protocol extensions

tldr.problem: The original RFCs defining Remote Direct Data Placement (RDDP) protocols did not create IANA registries for error codes, operation codes, and function codes, making it difficult to manage future protocol extensions.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC creates five IANA registries for RDDP: RDMAP Errors, DDP Errors, MPA Errors, RDMAP Message Operation Codes, and SCTP Function Codes for DDP Stream Session Control, each with initial values from the original specifications.
tldr.outcome: The registries enable managed allocation of code points for future RDDP protocol extensions while reserving experimental code points for research use.

today: RFC 6580 creates the IANA registries needed for RDDP protocol extensions. These registries are used by subsequent RDDP specifications such as RFC 6581 and enable organized allocation of code points for features like enhanced connection establishment.

sections.title: The Need for RDDP Code Registries
sections.content:
Remote Direct Data Placement (RDDP) is a suite of protocols that allow computers to transfer data directly to remote memory without involving the CPU of the receiving machine. The original RFCs (5040, 5041, 5043, 5044) defined the protocols but did not create IANA registries for code points.

As RDDP protocols are extended (such as in RFC 6581 and other upcoming specifications), new error codes, operation codes, and function codes need to be assigned in an organized way. This RFC creates the necessary IANA registries, populates them with values from the original specifications, and provides allocation policy guidance.
sections.eli5: RDDP lets computers send data directly to memory without the computer thinking about it. When things go wrong or new features are added, you need numbered codes. This RFC creates the official list and says how to add new codes.

sections.title: The RDDP Protocol Stack
sections.content:
The RDDP suite consists of multiple layers, each producing error codes:

RDMAP (Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol) operates at Layer 0 and produces 16-bit error codes divided into three subfields: a 4-bit Layer field (always 0x0), a 4-bit Error Type, and an 8-bit Error Code. Error codes are optional; when an Error Type alone is sufficient to specify the error, no Error Code is registered.

DDP (Direct Data Placement) operates at Layer 1 and uses the same 16-bit structure with Layer = 0x1. DDP distinguishes between Tagged Buffer errors and Untagged Buffer errors, plus a special entry reserving codes for the lower layer protocol.

MPA (Marker PDU Aligned Framing) operates at Layer 2 (0x2) and produces 16-bit error codes with a single Error Type and always requires a numeric Error Code.
sections.eli5: RDDP has three layers, each producing different kinds of error codes. Each layer is numbered (0, 1, 2) and has its own set of error types and specific error codes nested inside them.

sections.title: Message Operations and Function Codes
sections.content:
RDMAP Message Operation Codes are 4-bit values specifying what kind of message is being sent. The original RFCs define codes 0x0 through 0x7 for operations such as RDMA Write, RDMA Read Request, RDMA Read Response, Send, Send with Invalidate, Send with Solicited Event, and Terminate. Code 0xF is reserved for experimental use.

SCTP Function Codes for DDP Stream Session Control are 16-bit values used when DDP runs over SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol). The original specification defines codes 0x0001 through 0x0004 for operations like DDP Stream Session Initiate, Accept, Reject, and Terminate. Code 0xFFFF is reserved for experimental use.

Both registries allow any unassigned values to be allocated by future Standards-Track specifications.
sections.eli5: When RDDP sends a message, the first few bits say what kind of message it is (read, write, etc.). This RFC lists all those message types and how to add new ones in the future.

sections.title: Code Point Allocation Policy
sections.content:
All five registries use the same allocation policy: Standards Action. This means new code points can only be assigned through an IESG-approved Standards-Track RFC. Allocation requests should include a specification that defines the semantics and interoperability requirements of the proposed new code point.

When suggesting specific numerical values, allocation requests can note codes that early implementations have already chosen. If the IANA allocation request is accepted, such suggestions may be honored if the value is still available.

The RFC reserves specific experimental code points for use in research and prototyping. Code 0xF is reserved as experimental for RDMAP Message Operation Codes (allowing 4-bit experiments), and code 0xFFFF is reserved for SCTP Function Codes.
sections.eli5: Want to add a new code? You need to write a proper RFC that explains what the code does and why it's needed. This keeps the system organized and prevents random additions.

sections.title: Initial Registry Contents and Examples
sections.content:
The RDMAP Errors registry begins with entries like 0x0/0x0/ALL (Local Catastrophic Error) and 0x0/0x1/0x00 (Remote Protection Error / Invalid Steering Tag). The registry distinguishes between Error Types that require specific Error Codes (such as Remote Protection Error) and those that use a wildcard 'ALL' value for the Error Code field when no specific codes are registered.

The DDP Errors registry includes Tagged Buffer errors (Layer 1, Type 0x1), Untagged Buffer errors (Layer 1, Type 0x2), and notably reserves Layer 1, Type 0x3 entirely for use by the lower layer protocol with the special entry 0x1/0x3/ALL.

The MPA Errors registry is simpler, with four defined error types covering TCP connection issues, CRC errors, marker mismatches, and invalid frame formats.

All registries note that combinations not listed are Unassigned and available for IANA assignment by future Standards-Track specifications.
sections.eli5: Each registry lists the specific error codes and operation codes defined in the original RDDP RFCs. New codes can be added later by anyone who writes a proper standard.
